entities.name: Darius the Mede
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Darius the Mede, a figure whose historicity remains a subject of intense scholarly debate, is primarily known from the biblical Book of Daniel, where he is depicted as the ruler who succeeds Belshazzar after the fall of Babylon to the Medo-Persian forces around 539 BCE. Described as 'about sixty-two years old' at the time of his accession (Daniel 5:31), he represents a crucial transitional authority following the Neo-Babylonian Empire's collapse and preceding the full consolidation of Achaemenid Persian rule under Cyrus the Great. His existence challenges conventional historical and archaeological records, which do not explicitly name such a ruler between Nabonidus/Belshazzar and Cyrus in Babylon, making him a unique intersection point for ancient Near Eastern history and religious scholarship.

The Book of Daniel details Darius the Mede's brief but impactful reign over the 'kingdom of the Chaldeans,' including his administrative reorganization of the newly conquered territory into 120 satrapies with three chief administrators, one of whom was Daniel himself. His tenure is marked by the dramatic 'lion's den' episode, where Daniel is miraculously saved after being condemned for defying a royal decree prohibiting prayer to any god or man other than Darius for thirty days. This narrative underscores the tension between imperial authority and religious devotion, a recurring theme in the Persian period. The text also attributes to him the 'receiving' of the kingdom, suggesting an appointment or delegation of authority rather than a conquest.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Darius the Mede holds significant regional and thematic importance due to his pivotal role in the biblical Book of Daniel, which profoundly shaped Jewish and Christian understandings of imperial succession and divine intervention. His controversial historicity continues to drive scholarly debate, impacting the interpretation of ancient Near Eastern history.
